project.title: ChurnCast: End-to-End Data Science Case Study on Subscription Churn
project.tagline: Take a messy meal-subscription export from raw CSVs to a tested, leakage-free churn model that beats the retention team's rule of thumb, with grouped out-of-time validation, calibration and fairness checks, CI with an evaluation gate, a prediction API with an AI explainer, and monitoring and retraining after it goes live
project.description: TiffinBox, a meal-subscription startup, loses about 9 % of its paying customers every month, and its retention team can call only 10 % of them with an offer. Over nine phases you build the churn model they need, like a professional data science team: frame the decision and the label, write a data contract, a timeline and a modelling plan with ADRs, then build the pipeline test-first in your track: load four deliberately messy CSVs as text, apply documented cleaning rules that count every row they drop, check the contract, build point-in-time features that only use what was known at each month-end snapshot (and avoid the leaky cancellation_reason column), compare two baselines (the training churn rate and the team's five-flag rule) with two logistic regressions using grouped 5-fold cross-validation, then evaluate the champion once on out-of-time test months: AUC, average precision, Brier, calibration (ECE), precision and recall of the top-10 % call list, net value per month, slices, an age-band fairness check and a leakage scan, all behind a release gate. Golden files, invariants, leakage and contract-violation tests pin every number, and the Python, SQL and R tracks must agree (features to 1e-9, metrics and coefficients to 1e-6). CI executes the notebook or R Markdown report, runs the gate and checks parity; a generated model card and a FastAPI prediction API with an optional AI explainer (numbered facts in, guardrails out, a deterministic template as fallback) ship in Docker as v1.0.0. Then the model meets the real world: a new acquisition channel breaks the contract, prices change, and the deployed model's calibration slips. You version the contract, add drift (PSI) and realised-performance monitoring, recalibrate and retrain a challenger, decide champion vs challenger on a holdout month, add request ids, JSON logs and Prometheus metrics to the API, and write a blameless post-mortem (v1.1.0). Pick Python (pandas, scikit-learn, Jupyter), SQL (DuckDB) or R (tidymodels, R Markdown); the data, contract, golden files and API are shared. Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.

prerequisites.title: Git and the command line basics
One of: Python with pandas, SQL (GROUP BY, JOIN, window functions) or R with dplyr
Basic statistics and the idea of a classifier: probabilities, a train/test split, overfitting

outcomes: Frame a business request as a prediction problem: the decision, the unit, the snapshot, the label and what a wrong call costs
Write a data contract (schema, accepted values, checks with severities) and a modelling plan with ADRs before training anything
Build point-in-time features from messy event tables without leaking the future, and recognise a leaky column
Validate honestly: grouped cross-validation by customer and an out-of-time test set used once
Compare models with baselines first (prior and the team's rule of thumb), and choose a champion by a rule written in advance
Evaluate for the decision: ranking (AUC, AP), probabilities (Brier, calibration), the capacity-limited call list, value, slices and fairness
Pin a model with golden files, invariants, leakage and contract-violation tests, and make three implementations agree
Gate a release in GitHub Actions CI, generate a model card from the numbers, and serve the model with a FastAPI API in Docker
Add an AI explainer that only sees aggregate facts, is checked by guardrails and falls back to a deterministic template
Monitor a live model (PSI drift, realised performance), retrain and recalibrate a challenger, decide on a holdout and write a blameless post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every number they produce
project.ai_feature: An optional AI explainer in the prediction API: for one customer it receives only numbered facts (the churn probability, the base rate and the top feature contributions; never the customer id, raw records or a protected attribute) and writes a short note for a retention agent. Guardrails reject any answer with an unknown citation, a number that is not a correct rounding of a fact, a certainty claim ("will churn") or a sensitive attribute, and the API then returns a deterministic template instead. Offline by default; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (a local Ollama, or a free Gemini/Groq key) can be plugged in
project.portfolio_blurb: Built ChurnCast, an end-to-end churn model for a meal-subscription business on a deliberately messy export (customers, invoices, usage, support tickets): a versioned data contract with severity-graded checks, counted cleaning rules, point-in-time features at month-end snapshots (with a leakage scan that caught the cancellation_reason trap), two baselines and two logistic regressions compared with grouped 5-fold cross-validation, and an out-of-time test used once. The champion (test AUC 0.743, ECE 0.008) ranks the top-10 % call list 3.0x better than random, finds 30 % of next month's churners and is worth about ₹1.1 lakh a month against ₹63,000 for the team's rule of thumb, within an age-band recall gap of 0.12. Golden files, invariants and leakage tests; Python, SQL and R implementations that agree to 1e-6; a release gate and a generated model card in GitHub Actions CI; a FastAPI prediction API in Docker with a guard-railed AI explainer; and, after deployment, PSI drift and realised-performance monitoring that flagged a miscalibrated model, a recalibrated challenger promoted on a holdout month (Brier 0.119 → 0.113, ECE 0.059 → 0.013), request ids, JSON logs, Prometheus metrics and a blameless post-mortem (v1.1).

phases.title: Setup and the brief
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and the brief
phases.why_md:
A model nobody else can retrain is a rumour with a ROC curve. Professional data science teams start where
engineers start: a repository that installs with one command, data whose origin you can prove, tests that say what
"right" means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, read the brief and
the data, run the starter, meet the pending tests and the contract that will guide you, open your first pull
request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not train a single model yet, on purpose: first you learn which
decision the model serves and what the data can and cannot say.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Python, SQL or R), install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux, and run `make lint test`.
Explain the brief in two sentences: who decides what each month, with which capacity, and what a wrong call costs.

Prove the export in `data/raw/2026-05` is exactly the published one (`generate_data.py --check`) and list three defects you can see in the raw CSVs, plus the one column that must never become a feature.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/ds-case-study` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**. The
   `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/ds-case-study.git
   cd ds-case-study
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/ds-case-study.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/ds-case-study`), not under `/mnt/c`.

steps.title: Install the tools for ONE track
steps.content_md:
Every track needs Git, `make` and Python 3.12+ (the data generator, the parity script, the gate and, later, the API
are Python). Run the doctor script; it tells you exactly what is missing:
```bash
scripts/doctor.sh
```

<!-- track:python -->
**Python track:** pandas, scikit-learn and Jupyter, installed into a virtual environment with exact versions.
```bash
cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv with the pinned versions
.venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, sklearn; print(pandas.__version__, sklearn.__version__)"
```
Open the notebook with `.venv/bin/jupyter lab notebooks/churn-model.ipynb` (or VS Code with the Jupyter
extension, selecting `.venv` as the kernel).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL track:** DuckDB, an in-process analytical database: no server, it reads the CSVs directly. Cleaning,
features, labels and every metric are written in `sql/*.sql`; a thin Python runner sets variables, does the one
thing SQL cannot (fitting the logistic regression, with scikit-learn) and writes the JSON files.
```bash
cd tracks/sql && make install        # .venv with duckdb, scikit-learn, sqlfluff, pytest
.venv/bin/python -c "import duckdb; print(duckdb.sql(\"SELECT count(*) FROM '../../data/raw/2026-05/invoices.csv'\"))"
```
Optional: the DuckDB CLI (`brew install duckdb`, or the binary from duckdb.org) to explore by hand.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:r -->
**R track:** R 4.6 with tidymodels (parsnip, rsample, yardstick), dplyr, testthat, lintr and R Markdown. The
toolchain is a **Docker image** pinned to a dated CRAN snapshot, so you, your reviewer and CI run exactly the same
package versions. Build it once (about 5 minutes), then run every `make` target inside it:
```bash
docker build -f tracks/r/Dockerfile --target dev -t churncast-r-dev:local .
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/repo -w /repo/tracks/r churncast-r-dev:local Rscript -e 'packageVersion("parsnip")'
alias rdev='docker run --rm -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD":/repo -w /repo/tracks/r churncast-r-dev:local'
```
(Run the alias from the repository root.) RStudio users can still edit in RStudio; a local R 4.6 works with
`cd tracks/r && make install`, but CI uses the image, so check there before you push.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: Read the brief and the data
steps.content_md:
1. Read the top of `README.md` (the situation) and `contract/feature-spec.md` §1 (the problem and the timeline).
   Write down, in your own words: **who decides, what, how often, with which capacity, and what each kind of
   wrong call costs.**
2. Read `data/README.md`, then look at the raw files themselves. They are small on purpose:
   ```bash
   head -5 data/raw/2026-05/customers.csv
   grep -c '/' data/raw/2026-05/customers.csv           # rows with the day-first date format
   cut -d, -f3 data/raw/2026-05/customers.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -12   # city spellings
   grep -c '₹' data/raw/2026-05/invoices.csv            # amounts written as text with a rupee sign
   python3 scripts/generate_data.py --check             # byte-identical to the seeded generator
   ```
3. Note three defects you can see without any code (duplicate rows? two date formats? negative counts?). Phase 2
   turns each of them into a rule.
4. Look at `cancellation_reason` in `customers.csv`. When is it filled in? Why would a model that uses it look
   brilliant in testing and be useless in production? Write one sentence; Phase 3 M3 comes back to it.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant explained a `pip` / `duckdb` / Docker error
   during the install and how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my workflows, go
   ahead and enable them"**. CI runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks (the R job builds the same image you
   built). Wait for green, fill in the PR template and merge.

ai_prompts.title: Fix my toolchain install
ai_prompts.prompt:
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a <Python 3.12 with pandas,
scikit-learn and Jupyter | DuckDB 1.x from Python | R 4.6 in Docker (rocker/r-ver) with tidymodels> project.
Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh: <paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is missing,
explain each one in one line, and tell me how to verify each install.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running each verification command, re-running `scripts/doctor.sh` until every line for your track is green, and checking any download URL against the official site (python.org, duckdb.org, docs.docker.com, cloud.r-project.org). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

ai_prompts.title: Restate the brief as a decision
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a stakeholder brief: <paste the "situation" paragraph of README.md and feature-spec.md §1>.
Restate it as: (1) the decision to be made, by whom, how often, (2) the capacity constraint, (3) the cost of each
kind of wrong call, (4) what a model must output for that decision (a ranking? a probability? a reason?),
(5) three ways a model could look good in a notebook and still fail this team. Do not compute anything and do not
guess numbers that are not in the brief.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every claim against the brief (assistants add details that are not there, such as a churn rate per city or a budget), and keeping at least one failure mode about *time* (a model trained on the future, or a test set from the same months as the training data). You will design against it in Phase 2.

ai_prompts.title: Read a raw file like a data scientist
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are the header and 15 sample rows of a raw CSV export of a subscription business: <paste head -16
data/raw/2026-05/invoices.csv>. List every data-quality problem you can see or suspect, how you would detect each
one in code, which column could leak the outcome into a churn model, and what you would ask the data owner.
Do not clean anything yet.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: finding each problem in the real file with `grep` or a quick count (an assistant may "see" problems that are not in your sample), and comparing your list with `contract/feature-spec.md` §2. These rows are synthetic; with real customer data you would paste column names and aggregates only, never rows.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise the CSV files are not copied
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: The retention team can call 10 % of active customers a month. What does that mean for the model?
options: Only accuracy matters
The model must predict churn for exactly 10 % of customers
What matters most is how well it ranks the top 10 % of each month, plus honest probabilities for budgeting
The model is only useful if its AUC is above 0.9
quiz.explanation: A capacity-limited decision is a ranking problem: precision and recall of the call list matter more than accuracy at a 0.5 threshold. Finance also multiplies the probabilities by prices, so calibration matters too.

quiz.q: Why is `customers.cancellation_reason` never a feature?
options: It has too many missing values
It is text, and models need numbers
It is filled in after a customer cancels, so it encodes the outcome; at prediction time it is empty for everyone who has not left yet
It is a protected attribute
quiz.explanation: This is target leakage. A model using it would score superbly on historical data and be useless on the next month. The leakage scan in Phase 3 measures exactly how "good" it would look.

quiz.q: Why are all tests skipped in the starter?
options: They are flaky
CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you build in Phases 3-4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (test-first). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: What is `contract/fixtures/metric-cases.json` for?
options: Training data for the model
Tiny inputs with AUC, average precision, Brier and calibration worked out by hand, so a metric written from scratch can be checked exactly
A cache of scikit-learn's results
The golden metrics of the real export
quiz.explanation: Metrics are where silent bugs hide (ties in AUC, the last calibration bin). The cases pin every edge case; all three tracks must reproduce them.

quiz.q: Which of these may you paste into an AI prompt for this project?
options: Your `.env` file with an LLM API key
500 rows of a real customer invoices export

phases.title: Problem framing: the decision, the label and success criteria
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Problem framing: the decision, the label and success criteria
phases.why_md:
Most failed data science projects fail before the first line of code: the model predicts the wrong thing, at the
wrong time, for a decision nobody makes. "Predict churn" is not a problem statement. *Who* is scored, *when*, with
*which* data, *what* exactly counts as churn, and *what happens* to the people at the top of the list? In this
phase you turn the Head of Growth's question into a prediction problem with a unit, a snapshot, a label and a
horizon, write down what each kind of error costs, and agree success criteria **before** anyone sees a model
score, so that the evaluation cannot be bent later towards the model someone likes.
objectives: State the decision, its frequency and its capacity constraint, and the cost of a false alarm versus a missed churner.
Define the prediction problem precisely: one row per customer and month-end snapshot, label = no paid renewal next month.
Say which data may be used at prediction time and which may not (and why `cancellation_reason` and `age_band` are excluded from the features).
Write success criteria tied to the decision: beat the rule of thumb on the call list, honest probabilities, a fairness check.
Write requirements with at least eight testable acceptance criteria and five risks, and merge them as `spec/requirements.md`.

steps.title: The decision and its economics
steps.content_md:
1. Read `contract/feature-spec.md` §1 and the `evaluation` block of `contract/data-contract.yaml`
   (`top_percent`, `offer_cost_inr`, `save_rate`, `value_months`).
2. Work out the economics of one call by hand: a call + offer costs ₹200; if the customer would have churned and
   the offer saves 25 % of them, a saved customer is worth 3 months of their price. For a Standard customer at
   ₹3,299, what is the expected value of calling a true churner? Of calling someone who would have stayed?
3. Write the paragraph *The decision* in `spec/requirements.md`: who decides, monthly, 10 % capacity, the two
   kinds of error and which one is more expensive. Note that `save_rate` is an **assumption** nobody has measured.

steps.title: Unit, snapshot, label, horizon
steps.content_md:
Answer these in `spec/requirements.md` §3, then compare with `feature-spec.md` §3:
- **Unit:** one row = one customer at one month-end snapshot. Why not one row per customer?
- **Who is in a snapshot:** only customers with a *paid* charge for month M. Why not every customer ever?
- **Label:** churned = no paid charge for month M + 1. What about a failed payment that is retried? A refund?
- **Horizon:** one month. Why is "will this customer ever leave?" useless for a monthly call list?
- **Prediction time:** the end of month M. Which data exists then, and which (the label, the cancellation reason,
  a ticket created on the 3rd of M + 1) does not?

steps.title: Stakeholders and what they need
steps.content_md:
List at least four: the Head of Growth (who to call), retention agents (why this customer: a reason they can talk
about), finance (a budget: honest probabilities), the customers themselves (not treated differently because of
their age), and engineering (a model they can serve and roll back). For each, write what they need from the model
and what could go wrong for them.

steps.title: Success criteria, agreed before modelling
steps.content_md:
Write them as numbers with a reason each. The reference uses (`data-contract.yaml` → `gate`):

| Criterion | Threshold | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ranking on unseen months | test AUC ≥ 0.72 | below that, the call list is barely better than the rule |
| Beat the rule of thumb | AUC uplift ≥ 0.03 over B1 | otherwise keep the rule: it is free and everyone understands it |
| Honest probabilities | ECE ≤ 0.03 | finance multiplies them by prices |
| Better than a constant | Brier < the prior's Brier | a model that cannot beat the base rate is noise |
| Fair call list | age-band recall gap ≤ 0.15 | no age group may be systematically missed |
| No leakage | no single feature with AUC ≥ 0.90 | a feature that good is usually the label in disguise |

The champion is chosen by **cross-validation on the training months**, never by the test score; the test months
are used **once**.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria, risks, scope
steps.content_md:
1. At least eight testable acceptance criteria for the *pipeline* (reproducible from a clean checkout; every
   cleaning rule counted; an `error` check stops the run with exit code 3; no feature uses data after the cut-off;
   the three tracks agree; the gate blocks a bad model; the report runs top to bottom; the model card is generated).
2. At least five risks with a mitigation each: leakage, a random split that hides drift, over-confident
   probabilities, an unfair call list, a rule of thumb that is better than expected, an AI explanation that invents
   a number, a model that silently decays after launch.
3. Out of scope for v1: causal uplift modelling (who is *persuadable*), real-time scoring, other countries.
4. Commit on a branch, open a PR, merge when CI is green.

known before the first day of M+1. Act as a sceptical reviewer: list every way this label could be wrong or
misleading (failed payments, pauses, refunds, customers who come back, the last month of the export), say which
ones matter for a monthly call list, and propose a test for each. Do not suggest a different business.

the call list, value, fairness) and why each one serves this decision. Explain what AUC, precision@10 %, Brier and
expected calibration error each tell a business person, in one sentence each.

deliverables.text: `spec/requirements.md` with the decision, stakeholders, the prediction problem, success criteria, data limits, at least 8 acceptance criteria, at least 5 risks and the scope.
Your worked example of the economics of one call (in the requirements or the PR).
A merged PR with green CI, and an `AI_LOG.md` entry for any prompt you used.

quiz.q: Why is the unit "one customer at one month-end snapshot" rather than "one customer"?
options: It makes the dataset bigger, which always helps
The decision is made every month with what is known at that month's end, so the model must learn from the same situation, many times per customer
Customers change their id every month
Logistic regression needs at least 10,000 rows
quiz.explanation: The model must reproduce the moment of decision. A customer appears in every month they pay for; each row only knows the past of that month. (That is also why folds must keep a customer's rows together.)

quiz.q: Which data may a feature for snapshot M use?
options: Anything in the export
Anything about the customer, including `cancellation_reason`
Only what was known before the first instant of month M + 1: invoices and usage up to M, tickets created before then, resolutions that happened before then
Only month M itself
quiz.explanation: The cut-off S = first instant of M + 1. Anything later (the label month, a later resolution, the cancellation reason) is the future. Using it is leakage.

quiz.q: Why is the test set the *last* months rather than a random 20 % of rows?
options: Random splits are not supported by scikit-learn
The model will always be used on future months; a random split lets it learn from the same months it is tested on and hides drift
The last months have more churners
It is faster
quiz.explanation: An out-of-time test answers the real question: does a model trained on the past work next month? A random split usually overestimates performance.

quiz.q: Why must the model beat the rule of thumb (B1), not just the prior (B0)?
options: The rule is what the team does today for free; a model is only worth its cost and complexity if it does better on the same call list
The prior is always 0.5
The rule uses more features than the model
Beating B0 is impossible
quiz.explanation: The relevant comparison is the current process. The gate requires an AUC uplift of at least 0.03 over B1.

quiz.q: Finance multiplies the predicted probabilities by plan prices. Which property must the probabilities have?
options: They must sum to 1 across customers
They must be above 0.5 for churners
They must be calibrated: among customers given 20 %, about 20 % churn (low ECE)
They must be rounded to two decimals
quiz.explanation: A model can rank well (high AUC) and still be over- or under-confident. Calibration is measured with the expected calibration error and a reliability table.

quiz.q: Why are the success criteria written down before any model is trained?
options: The contract format requires it
So that the test set can be used to tune them
So that the evaluation cannot be bent after seeing results towards the model someone prefers (the garden of forking paths)
Because thresholds never change
quiz.explanation: Criteria chosen after seeing scores tend to be chosen to pass. Pre-registration is the cheapest protection against fooling yourself.

recap: A business request becomes a prediction problem through five choices: unit, snapshot, label, horizon, and prediction-time data.
Capacity turns churn into a ranking problem; budgeting adds calibration; people add fairness.
Errors have prices: the economics of one call tell you which metric matters.
Success criteria and the champion rule are agreed before modelling, and the test months are used once.

phases.title: Design: data contract, timeline, modelling plan and ADRs
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: data contract, timeline, modelling plan and ADRs
phases.why_md:
Two analysts given the same export and the same question will build different models, and both will believe their
own. The design phase makes the choices explicit and reviewable *before* the code: what a valid export looks like
(the data contract), which months train and which test (the timeline), which models are compared and how the
winner is picked (the modelling plan), and why each important decision was taken (ADRs). In this project the
design has one more job: the Python, SQL and R tracks must compute the same features to 1e-9, which is only
possible if every rule is written down exactly.
objectives: Read and extend a data contract: files, columns, cleaning rules, checks with `error`/`warn` severities, features, experiments, gate.
Draw the timeline: 6 training snapshots, 2 out-of-time test snapshots, the label month, the cut-off of each snapshot.
Explain grouped cross-validation (fold = customer number mod 5) and why a random K-fold would leak.
Write a modelling plan: two baselines, two logistic regressions, the champion rule, metrics and the gate.
Record at least four decisions as ADRs (text-first loading, point-in-time features, validation design, the model family, fairness).

steps.title: The data contract, line by line
steps.content_md:
Open `contract/data-contract.yaml` next to `contract/feature-spec.md` §2. For each block, write one sentence in
your notes on what would break without it:
- `files`: the four tables, their keys and columns. A missing column is a contract error (exit 3).
- `cleaning`: date and timestamp formats (day first!), city aliases, `missing_label`, `rating_default`.
- `leaky_columns`, `protected_columns`: never features. `age_band` is used only for the fairness check.
- `checks`: 21 checks. Which ones are `warn` and why? (`customers.channel.missing_share` is a quality signal,
  not a reason to stop; an unknown city or plan would silently create a new category, so it is an `error`.)
Then answer: the June export adds a new acquisition channel. What happens? (You will live through it in Phase 7.)

steps.title: The timeline and the splits
steps.content_md:
Draw it, on paper or in Markdown, for the 2026-05 export:
```text
2025-01 ......... 2025-09 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 2026-01 | 02 || 03 | 04 || 05
history only       train snapshots (6)                     test (2)    label month of 2026-04 only
```
1. Each snapshot M has a cut-off S = the first instant of M + 1 and a label from month M + 1.
2. Why does the first training snapshot start in 2025-09 rather than 2025-01? (Features look back up to three
   months and `tenure_months` needs history; the very first months have almost no customers.)
3. Folds: `fold = customer number mod 5`. All snapshots of a customer are in one fold. Why would a plain
   `KFold(shuffle=True)` overestimate AUC here? (The same customer, one month apart, sits on both sides.)
4. The test months are scored **once**, after the champion is chosen.

steps.title: The modelling plan
steps.content_md:
Write `spec/modelling-plan.md` (the template has six sections):
- **Baselines:** B0 = the training churn rate for everyone (the floor); B1 = the team's five risk flags, each
  flag count mapped to its training churn rate (the bar to beat).
- **Candidates:** E1 = logistic regression on the 5 `core` features; E2 = logistic regression on all 15.
- **Why logistic regression first:** probabilities that are usually well calibrated, coefficients in business
  units ("each extra open ticket adds … to the log-odds"), exact per-feature explanations, and three tracks can
  reproduce it exactly (unpenalised maximum likelihood has one answer). A gradient-boosted model may be a later
  experiment, judged by the same gate.
- **Champion rule:** E2 only if its mean CV AUC beats E1 by at least 0.002 (`champion.min_cv_auc_gain_for_complexity`).
- **Metrics and gate:** copy them from the requirements; add what each tells the business.
- **What stops a release:** any gate check failing, an `error` contract check, or parity failing between tracks.

steps.title: ADRs
steps.content_md:
Use `spec/adr/0000-template.md`. The reference has five; write at least four:
1. **Read raw files as text** and parse every type by an explicit rule (type guessing hides defects).
2. **Point-in-time features at month-end snapshots** with a single cut-off S, and a leakage scan in the gate.
3. **Validation design:** grouped 5-fold CV by customer on the training months + an out-of-time test used once.
4. **Unpenalised logistic regression with baselines first**, the champion by a pre-agreed CV rule.
5. **Fairness and protected attributes:** `age_band` is never a feature; the recall gap of the call list across
   age bands is a gate check.

quiz.q: Why is fold membership derived from the customer id rather than assigned at random per row?
options: It is faster to compute
All snapshots of a customer must sit in the same fold, or the model validates on customers it trained on one month earlier
Random numbers differ between Python and R
scikit-learn requires it
quiz.explanation: Rows of the same customer are strongly correlated. Grouped folds keep them together; `customers_in_two_folds` must be 0. (A deterministic rule also lets the three tracks use the same folds.)

quiz.q: An unknown city appears in an export. Why is that an `error` check and not a warning?
options: Cities are protected attributes
It would silently create a new category or a missing city tier, changing features without anyone noticing; stopping is cheaper than a wrong model
Error checks are faster
The model uses the city as a feature
quiz.explanation: Severity reflects the cost of continuing. A missing-channel share above 15 % is worth a warning; an unknown value in a category the pipeline maps is a contract break.

quiz.q: Why compare against B1 (the rule of thumb) at all?
options: It is required by scikit-learn
It always loses
It is the current process; if the model cannot beat it clearly, keeping the rule is cheaper and easier to explain
It provides the training labels
quiz.explanation: Baselines anchor the evaluation. B0 shows what "no information" scores; B1 shows what the team already achieves.

quiz.q: Why is unpenalised logistic regression a good first model here?
options: It always has the highest AUC
It gives usually well-calibrated probabilities, coefficients in business units, exact per-feature explanations, and one reproducible answer across tracks
It needs no features
It cannot overfit
quiz.explanation: With 15 features and ~12,000 rows, a linear model is a strong, transparent baseline. More complex models must beat it through the same gate.

quiz.q: What is an ADR for?
options: Listing the bugs found in review
Recording one important decision, the options considered and its consequences, so a later reader knows why things are the way they are
Documenting the API
Storing the hyper-parameters
quiz.explanation: Architecture (or analysis) Decision Records are short, dated and never rewritten: a later decision supersedes an earlier one.

quiz.q: Why does `age_band` appear in the contract at all if it is never a feature?
options: For the data dictionary only
To measure fairness: the recall of the call list must not differ by more than 0.15 across age bands
Because the model needs it to be accurate
It is a leaky column
quiz.explanation: Removing a protected attribute from the features does not make a model fair (other features can act as proxies). You must still measure outcomes by group.

The timeline (snapshots, cut-offs, labels, out-of-time test) and grouped folds are the backbone of an honest evaluation.
A modelling plan written before training: baselines, candidates, a champion rule, metrics and a gate.
ADRs capture the why behind decisions such as text-first loading, point-in-time features and fairness checks.

phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in five milestones: clean, check, features, models, evaluation
phases.why_md:
This is where most churn models quietly go wrong: a duplicated invoice that doubles a failed payment, a ticket from
next month that "predicts" this month's churn, a fold that shares customers, an AUC function that mishandles ties,
a test set peeked at to pick the winner. You build the pipeline **test-first**, one milestone at a time: delete a
line from the pending list, watch its tests fail, implement until they pass. Every function has a `TODO` with a
hint that says where in `contract/feature-spec.md` to look and which trap to avoid. At the end, one command turns
the raw export into `features.csv`, `metrics.json`, `model.json` and `experiments.jsonl`, and your numbers match the
golden files.
objectives: Load messy CSVs as text and apply the cleaning rules in order, counting every row they drop or change (M1).
Run the contract's checks with severities and stop on an `error` with exit code 3 (M2).
Build month-end snapshots, labels and 15 point-in-time features without leaking the future (M3).
Fit the two baselines and two logistic regressions with grouped 5-fold CV, and compute AUC, average precision, Brier, log loss and calibration from scratch (M4).
Choose the champion by the CV rule, evaluate it once on the test months (call list, value, slices, fairness, leakage, gate), write the artefact, and fill in the report (M5).

3. Implement one function at a time, re-running the tests (green). Commit after each green step:
   `feat(python): M1 parse money and dates`.
4. Never edit a test to make it pass. If you believe a test is wrong, open an issue quoting the spec section.

steps.title: M1 · Load and clean (`test_load`, `test_clean`)
steps.content_md:
Read `feature-spec.md` §2. Implement loading **as text**, then the four cleaners in the written order:
- customers: invalid signup dates → exact duplicates → city aliases and tiers → `unknown` channel and age band;
- invoices: exact duplicates → money parsing (`₹3,299`, `3,299.00`, `-150.00`) → month index → orphans;
- usage: exact duplicates → negative counts → orphans;
- tickets: invalid `created_at` → resolutions before creation set to missing → orphans.
Every rule adds to `issues`. On the tiny fixture the expected counts are in `contract/fixtures/tiny-expected.json`.
On the real export you will see: 3 invalid signup dates, 71 duplicate customers, 508 missing channels, 148
duplicate invoices, 59 rows with negative usage, 31 tickets resolved before they were created, and more.

steps.content_md:
Implement the six check types of `data-contract.yaml` (`unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values`, `range`,

steps.title: M3 · Point-in-time snapshots, labels and features (`test_features`)
steps.content_md:
The heart of the project (`feature-spec.md` §3-§4). For each snapshot month M:
1. **Who:** customers with a paid charge for M (one per customer: the lowest `invoice_id`).
2. **Label:** 1 if no paid charge for M + 1; null if M + 1 is not in the export.
3. **Features:** only what was known before S = first instant of M + 1. A ticket created at 00:00 on the 1st of
   M + 1 is invisible; a ticket resolved after S is still *open* at S. Usage of a missing month counts as zero.
4. `split` and `fold` from the contract; sort by snapshot, then `customer_id`.
Check your summary: 8 snapshots, from 1,608 rows (2025-09) to 2,652 rows (2026-04), churn rates between 8.5 % and
10.7 %; 11,862 training rows and 5,148 test rows.

steps.title: M4 · Baselines, logistic regression, grouped CV and the metrics (`test_model`, `test_metrics`)
steps.content_md:

   average ranks for ties, average precision over distinct scores, Brier, log loss with clipping, 10-bin
   calibration and ECE, `top_k = ceil(n · 10 / 100)` in integers.

   linear predictor is added up feature by feature (the hint explains the BLAS tie trap).

quiz.q: A ticket was created on 2026-03-01 00:00. Which snapshot can see it?
options: 2026-02 (it is about February's service)
2026-03 and later, never 2026-02: its cut-off is 2026-03-01 00:00 and a feature may only use tickets created strictly before it
Every snapshot of that customer
None: tickets at midnight are invalid
quiz.explanation: The cut-off of snapshot M is the first instant of M + 1. "Created < S" excludes the ticket from 2026-02. Boundary tests like this one catch most leaks.

quiz.q: Why must the logistic regression be unpenalised (`C=inf`) in this project?
options: Penalised models cannot produce probabilities
Unpenalised maximum likelihood has one answer every library finds, so the tracks can be compared to 1e-6; defaults of penalised fits differ by library
Penalties always reduce AUC
It trains faster
quiz.explanation: scikit-learn defaults to L2 with C=1; R's glm is unpenalised. With 15 features and ~12,000 rows the penalty is not needed, and parity requires the same model.

quiz.q: E1 has a slightly better test call list than E2, but E2 is the champion. Why not switch?
options: E2 has more features, so it must be better
The champion was chosen in advance by the CV rule; choosing by test score turns the test months into a second validation set and the reported numbers become optimistic
E1 failed the gate
The test months are not labelled
quiz.explanation: The test set is used once, for an honest report. Record the observation as a limitation, and let a future experiment (with a new test period) decide.

quiz.q: What does an AUC of about 0.88 for "cancellation_reason is filled" tell you?
options: It is the best feature and should be added
It is a near-perfect proxy for the outcome, known only after the customer cancels: target leakage
The column has missing values
Customers who give a reason are less likely to churn
quiz.explanation: The leakage scan reports it on purpose to show how good a leak looks. A real feature set should have nothing near it (the reference maximum is 0.70).

quiz.q: Why are AUC and calibration implemented from scratch instead of calling a library?
options: Libraries are slow
Three tracks must agree exactly, and libraries differ on ties, class order and bin edges; the spec plus the metric cases pin one definition
Libraries cannot compute ECE
It is required by the licence
quiz.explanation: Writing a metric once, testing it on hand-computed cases and comparing it across implementations is how you discover the edge cases (ties, one-class slices, p = 1 in the last bin).

quiz.q: Your pipeline's `issues.invoices_exact_duplicates` is 0 on the real export. What is the most likely bug?
options: The export has no duplicates
Duplicates were removed by the CSV reader
Money was parsed before deduplication (so `₹3,299` and `3,299.00` copies look different), or deduplication used a subset of columns
The test fixture is wrong
quiz.explanation: Rule order matters: exact duplicates are removed on the raw text first (148 rows on the real export). Every count is pinned so that an order mistake shows up immediately.

phases.title: Testing data and models: golden files, invariants, leakage, parity
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing data and models: golden files, invariants, leakage, parity
phases.why_md:
Unit tests on a tiny fixture prove that each rule does what it says. They do not prove that the whole pipeline,
on the real export, produces the model you think it does, or that the next refactor will not move a number. Data
and model tests close that gap: **golden files** pin every output, **invariants** state truths that must hold for
any export, **leakage tests** try to smuggle the future in, **contract-violation tests** feed broken exports and
expect the run to stop, and **model-quality tests** encode the release criteria. On top, three independent
implementations must agree. When all of this is green you can change code without fear, which is what Phase 7
will ask of you.
objectives: Explain the difference between unit, data, model and parity tests, and what each one catches.
Pin `metrics.json` and `model.json` to golden files with tolerances that match the maths (1e-6 for fits, 1e-9 for features).
Write invariants: rows read = kept + dropped, features inside their contract range, one row per customer and snapshot, contributions that add up to the prediction.
Prove there is no leakage: adding future rows to an export must not change any past feature.
Reach the 85 % line-coverage gate with unit + data tests, and show that training twice gives identical results.

steps.title: Golden files and tolerances
steps.content_md:
`test_golden` compares your run with `contract/golden/metrics-2026-05.json` and `model-2026-05.json` through
`scripts/parity.py` (`feature-spec.md` §8): integers, strings, booleans and list lengths exactly; floats to 1e-6
absolute + relative. Why not exact? Two optimisers (Newton-Cholesky, IRLS) converge to the same maximum, not to
the same last bit. Why not 1e-3? Because a real bug (a wrong rule, a missed row) usually moves a number by much
more than 1e-6 and much less than 1e-3. Read `parity.py`'s output on a deliberately broken run: it prints every
differing path.

steps.title: Invariants
Leakage and contract violations
steps.content_md:
- `test_rows_from_the_future_do_not_change_past_features` copies the export, appends invoices, usage and tickets
  dated *after* each snapshot, re-runs, and expects every past feature to be identical. This is the strongest
  leakage test you can write: it does not need to know where the leak would be.
- `test_the_leaky_column_would_have_looked_like_the_best_feature`: the probe AUC must be higher than every real
  feature's, and `cancellation_reason` must not appear in the artefact.
- `test_contract_violations` breaks a copy of the export four ways (an unknown plan, a reused invoice id, an export
  with no renewals, an impossible meal count) and expects **exit code 3** with the failing check's id.

steps.title: Model quality and determinism
steps.content_md:
`test_model_quality` encodes Phase 1's criteria: the gate passes; the champion beats B0 and B1; the champion was
chosen on CV, not on the test months; CV is stable (SD of fold AUCs small); calibration and fairness within
limits; the campaign is worth more than the rule; and **training twice gives identical results**.

steps.content_md:

```bash
python3 scripts/parity.py contract/golden/metrics-2026-05.json tracks/*/out/metrics.json
```

linear-predictor hint), the parity check found a real bug in one track before any user did.

quiz.q: Why are golden files compared with a tolerance of 1e-6 rather than exactly?
options: JSON cannot store exact floats
Different optimisers converge to the same maximum-likelihood estimate but not to the last bit; 1e-6 is far tighter than any real bug and looser than solver noise
To make the tests pass more often
Because the data is synthetic
quiz.explanation: Tolerances must match the maths. Features are plain arithmetic and are compared to 1e-9; fitted numbers to 1e-6.

quiz.q: What does "rows read = rows kept + rows dropped" protect against?
options: Slow pipelines
A rule that silently drops or duplicates rows without counting them, for example a join that fans out
Missing values in features
Wrong AUC
quiz.explanation: Every cleaning rule counts what it removes. If the accounting does not balance, some step changed the row count without saying so.

quiz.q: Why does the leakage test append *future* rows instead of checking each feature's SQL or code?
options: It is shorter
It does not need to know where a leak could be: any feature that changes when only the future changes is using the future
It tests the CSV reader
Future rows are invalid and must be rejected
quiz.explanation: It is a metamorphic test: a transformation of the input (adding the future) with a known effect on the output (none on the past).

quiz.q: A broken export has an unknown plan `family`. What should happen?
options: The rows with that plan are dropped and counted
The plan is mapped to `basic`
The `invoices.plan.accepted` error check fails and the run stops with exit code 3, naming the check
The model trains without the plan features
quiz.explanation: An unknown category would silently change the plan features. Stopping is the safe default; the contract decides, not the code.

quiz.q: Why test that training twice gives identical results?
options: To measure speed
Non-determinism (random seeds, thread-dependent sums, unordered groupbys) makes every other comparison unreliable and a model impossible to audit
Because CI runs twice
It checks the coverage gate
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility is a precondition for golden files and parity. The SQL track pins DuckDB to one thread for the same reason.

quiz.q: Python and SQL agree on every metric, R differs only in average precision by 5e-6. What is the most likely cause?
options: R cannot compute average precision
Two rows with identical features score a last bit apart in one track, so a tie is broken differently; check how the linear predictor is summed
The golden file is wrong
R rounds floats to 5 decimals
quiz.explanation: Ranking metrics are sensitive to ties. Summing the linear predictor feature by feature (not with a BLAS matrix product) gives bit-identical scores for identical rows in every track.

recap: The test pyramid for data science: unit (rules), data (real export), model (release criteria), parity (implementations).
Golden files with tolerances that match the maths, and how to read a difference.
Invariants, metamorphic leakage tests and contract-violation tests that need no knowledge of the bug.
Determinism as a requirement, and why three implementations are a powerful test.

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions and the evaluation gate
phases.heading: Phase 5 · CI with GitHub Actions and the evaluation gate
phases.why_md:
A model release is a code release with an extra failure mode: the code can be fine and the model worse. CI turns
your tests, the release criteria and the cross-track parity into a check on every pull request, run on a clean
machine that has never seen your laptop's cached files. In this phase you replace the starter's lint-and-unit CI
with the full pipeline: path filters so only affected tracks run, a reusable workflow per track, data and model
tests with a coverage gate, the run, schema validation, the **evaluation gate**, the report executed top to bottom,
parity with the golden files, and a single required check. The R track runs inside its pinned image, so "works on
my machine" and "works in CI" mean the same thing.
objectives: Read and modify `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `reusable-track-ci.yml` (triggers, jobs, `needs`, `if`, matrix, reusable workflows).
Run a track's full check in CI: lint → unit → coverage gate → run → schema validation → evaluation gate → report.
Build and cache a Docker toolchain image in CI and run `make` inside it.
Compare every track's outputs with the golden files in a `parity` job using artifacts.
Protect `main` with the `ci-ok` aggregator check, and explain why a failing gate must block a merge.

steps.content_md:

branch, set `min_test_auc: 0.80` in the contract, push, and watch the gate step go red with the line
`FAIL  test_auc  value 0.7430  threshold 0.8000`. Then revert. Discuss in the PR: who is allowed to change a threshold, and when?
(Answer from Phase 1: the people who agreed the success criteria, with a reason, in a contract change.)

steps.title: Parity, the contract job and the aggregator
steps.content_md:
- `parity` downloads every `run-*` artifact, reads the export month from a `metrics.json` and runs `parity.py`
  against `contract/golden/metrics-<export>.json` and `model-<export>.json`, then compares the `features.csv`
  files with each other. It runs if at least one track succeeded.
- `contract` (when shared files or docs change): `generate_data.py --check`, the golden files validate against
  their schemas and pass the gate, ruff and shellcheck on `scripts/`, and `build-cms.py --check`.
- `ci-ok` needs every job, runs `if: always()`, and fails only on `failure` or `cancelled`: skipped jobs (a
  docs-only PR) are fine.

quiz.q: Why does the path filter live inside the workflow (a `changes` job) instead of `on: push: paths:`?
options: `paths:` is deprecated
A workflow skipped by `paths:` never reports its checks, so a required check would block the PR forever; jobs that are skipped by `if:` still let the aggregator report
`paths:` does not work with pull requests
It is faster
quiz.explanation: The aggregator pattern (`ci-ok` with `if: always()`) gives one stable required check whatever was skipped.

quiz.q: Why does a change in `contract/` or `data/` re-run every track?
options: To use more CI minutes
Every track's numbers depend on the contract and the data, so all three must prove they still match
Because the R image must be rebuilt
GitHub requires it
quiz.explanation: `shared` paths fan out to every track. A contract change without all three tracks updated is caught here.

quiz.q: Why run the R track inside a Docker image instead of installing R on the runner?
options: R cannot be installed on Ubuntu
The image pins R, tidymodels and lintr to the versions you use locally, so a package update cannot move a coefficient or a lint rule between your laptop and CI
Docker is faster than installing R
GitHub forbids R on runners
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility of the toolchain is part of the reproducibility of the model. The image is built from a dated CRAN snapshot and cached between runs.

quiz.q: The evaluation gate fails in CI because test AUC dropped from 0.743 to 0.712 after your change. What do you do?
options: Lower `min_test_auc` to 0.70 in the same PR
Add `continue-on-error: true` to the gate step
Find out why the model got worse (a rule changed? a feature lost?), and only change a threshold through a reviewed contract change with a reason
Re-run the job until it passes
quiz.explanation: The gate encodes the success criteria agreed in Phase 1. It is there precisely to stop a worse model from shipping.

quiz.q: How do jobs share the tracks' outputs with the `parity` job?
options: Through the runner's disk
Through environment variables
Each track uploads an artifact (`run-<track>`), and `parity` downloads them with `actions/download-artifact`
Through a database service
quiz.explanation: Every job runs on a fresh machine; artifacts are the way to pass files between jobs (and to download them after the run).

quiz.q: What does `cancel-in-progress: true` in `concurrency` do?
options: Cancels failed jobs
A new push to the same branch cancels the older run of that branch, saving minutes on outdated commits
Prevents two branches from running at the same time
Cancels the deploy workflow
quiz.explanation: The group is per workflow and ref; only the latest commit of a branch matters.

recap: A CI pipeline for a modelling project: tests, the run, schema validation, the evaluation gate, executed reports, parity.
Reusable workflows, path filters with an aggregator check, artifacts, caching, and a Docker toolchain in CI.
Branch protection with one required check, and why the gate must be able to block a merge.

phases.heading: Phase 6 · Model card, prediction API, AI explainer, Docker and delivery
phases.why_md:
A model in a notebook helps nobody on Monday morning. The retention team needs a ranked list with a reason per
customer; engineering needs something they can run, monitor and roll back; everyone needs an honest description of
what the model is for and where it fails. In this phase you ship v1.0.0: a **model card** generated from the
numbers (so it cannot drift from the model), a **prediction API** that serves any track's `model.json` with
per-customer explanations, an optional **AI explainer** that turns the explanation into a sentence an agent can
use and that is not allowed to invent anything, and **Docker images** for the API and the three pipelines,
checked in CI and published to GHCR on a version tag.
objectives: Generate a model card (intended use, data, metrics, calibration, slices, fairness, limits) and check in CI that it matches the golden files.
Run and test the FastAPI prediction API: `/health`, `/v1/model`, `/v1/predict`, `/v1/explain`, problem+json errors, a small HTML form.
Explain the explainer's safety design: numbered facts in, guardrails out, a deterministic template as fallback, offline by default.
Build small, non-root, read-only images and run the three pipelines plus parity with `docker compose --profile train`.
Release v1.0.0: CHANGELOG, a tag, images on GHCR, a runbook, and an optional free Render deploy.

steps.title: The model card
steps.content_md:
```bash
python3 scripts/model_card.py tracks/python/out/metrics.json tracks/python/out/model.json > docs/model-card.md
python3 scripts/model_card.py --check docs/model-card.md contract/golden/metrics-2026-05.json contract/golden/model-2026-05.json
```
Read the generated card critically. The numbers come from the files; the words (intended use, out-of-scope uses,
limits, ethics) are in the script. Check that it says, at least: the model ranks customers for a capacity-limited
call list, it is **not** evidence that a call causes anyone to stay (`save_rate` is an assumption to test with a
randomised hold-out group), it was evaluated on two months only, and `age_band` is used for the fairness check only.
Add the release recommendation in your own words to the PR: ship E2 to the call list, run a hold-out experiment

steps.title: The prediction API
steps.content_md:
The API is provided: bring it in from the reference, then read and run it.
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags && git checkout phase-6-end -- serving models
cd serving && make install lint coverage
MODEL_PATH=../models/churncast-1.0.0.json make serve      # http://127.0.0.1:8000, docs at /docs
```
- `POST /v1/predict` takes up to 1,000 customers (`{"customers": [{"customer_id": "...", "features": {...}}]}`),
  validates every feature against its contract range (out of range → **422** `application/problem+json` naming
  the field), and returns the probability, the risk band (`high` above `high_risk_threshold`) and the top reasons.
- `POST /v1/explain` returns the contributions and a note: the template by default.
- `models/churncast-1.0.0.json` is the Python track's artefact, released as the v1.0 model. The API loads any
  1.x artefact of any track: try `MODEL_PATH=../tracks/r/out/model.json`.

steps.title: The AI explainer, safely
steps.content_md:
Read `serving/churncast_api/explainer.py` top to bottom. The model never sees a customer id, raw records or a
protected attribute: only numbered facts (`R1: open support tickets = 2, adds +0.31 to the log-odds`, the
probability, the base rate). Its answer must pass four guardrails: plain text within 600 characters citing at
least two existing facts; every number a correct rounding of a fact; no certainty claims ("will churn"); no
sensitive attributes. Otherwise the API returns the template with `fallback: true` and a reason.
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 LLM_MODEL=llama3.2 make serve   # optional: a local Ollama
```
The tests run the explainer against a fake LLM server that returns good, invented-number, overconfident and
slow answers. No API key is ever needed.

quiz.q: Why is the model card generated from `metrics.json` and `model.json` instead of written by hand?
options: Markdown is hard to write
Every number then comes from the model it describes, and CI's `--check` fails if the card and the model drift apart
The site requires JSON
It is shorter
quiz.explanation: Hand-copied numbers go stale after the first retrain. The words around the numbers are reviewed in the script.

quiz.q: The model card says the campaign is worth about ₹1.1 lakh a month. What is the biggest caveat?
options: The prices are in rupees
It assumes a 25 % save rate that nobody has measured; a randomised hold-out group is needed to know whether calls cause customers to stay
The AUC is too low
It only covers the Python track
quiz.explanation: A churn model predicts who is at risk, not who can be persuaded. The value estimate is only as good as the save-rate assumption.

quiz.q: Which of these does the AI explainer receive?
options: The customer id and their last three invoices
The customer's age band, to personalise the message
Numbered facts: the probability, the base rate and the top feature contributions
The whole training set
quiz.explanation: Data minimisation by construction: the explainer can only talk about the facts it is given, and guardrails check that it did.

quiz.q: The LLM answers "This customer will churn because of 3 late deliveries" but the fact says 2. What happens?
options: The answer is returned as is
The API returns 500
Two guardrails fail (a certainty claim and a number that is not in the facts), so the API returns the template with `fallback: true` and the reason
The number is corrected automatically
quiz.explanation: The API never shows an unchecked model answer. The template is always available, even when the provider is down.

quiz.q: Why do the containers run as a non-root user with a read-only file system?
options: It makes them faster
If the process is compromised, it cannot modify the image's code or write outside the mounted output and `/tmp`, which limits the damage
Docker requires it
So that the model cannot be retrained
quiz.explanation: Least privilege applies to containers too. The compose file sets `read_only: true` and a `tmpfs` for `/tmp`; the images create uid 10001.

quiz.q: Why can the API serve a `model.json` produced by the R track?
options: The API contains an R interpreter
The artefact is a language-neutral JSON file defined by `contract/model.schema.json`: features, coefficients, means, threshold
R models are converted to Python with a library
It cannot; only Python models work
quiz.explanation: A shared artefact contract decouples training from serving. The Docker job in CI proves it by serving the R model it just trained.

recap: A model card that is generated, checked and honest about intended use, causality and limits.
A small, validated prediction API with explanations that are exact for a linear model.
A safe AI feature: data minimisation, guardrails, a deterministic fallback, offline by default, tested against a fake LLM.
Docker images that are small, non-root and read-only, compose profiles, and continuous delivery to GHCR on a tag.

phases.title: Monitoring, drift, retraining and a post-mortem
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Monitoring, drift, retraining and a post-mortem
phases.why_md:
A model is evaluated once and then lives for months in a world that keeps changing. Marketing launches a new
channel, finance raises prices, churn rises, and a model that was well calibrated in March starts under-predicting
in June while its AUC still looks fine. In this phase the v1.0 model meets that world. The July export **breaks the
pipeline** (a new acquisition channel fails the data contract), and once that is fixed, monitoring shows drift and
a calibration problem. You version the contract, add drift (PSI) and realised-performance monitoring, retrain and
recalibrate a challenger, decide champion versus challenger on a month neither has seen, make the API observable
(request ids, JSON logs, metrics), and write a blameless post-mortem. That is v1.1.0.
objectives: Diagnose a contract failure from the exit code and the failing check, and fix it with a versioned contract change rather than a code hack.
Compute the population stability index (PSI) of every feature and of the score against the training reference, and classify stable / watch / drift.
Measure the deployed model's realised performance on newly labelled months, and explain why calibration can fail while AUC holds.
Retrain and recalibrate a challenger, and promote it only through a pre-agreed champion/challenger gate on a holdout month.
Add request ids, structured logs and Prometheus metrics to the API without logging personal data, and write a blameless post-mortem.

steps.title: The July export breaks the pipeline
steps.content_md:
Take the new export from the reference and run v1.0 on it:
```bash
git checkout phase-7-end -- data/raw/2026-07
make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-07       # R: rdev make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-07
# contract error: contract check(s) failed: customers.channel.accepted      (exit 3)
```
Investigate before you fix: which value is new (`influencer`, launched by marketing in June 2026), how many
customers, since when. The contract did its job: it stopped a model from silently treating a new channel as
something else. Now decide **in the contract**, with a version bump to 1.1.0: add `influencer` to the accepted
values (the channel is not a model feature, so the model is unaffected; the slices and the fairness check see it).
Keep 1.0.0 in `contract/history/` and log the incident timeline for the post-mortem.

steps.title: Post-deployment snapshots and monitoring
steps.content_md:
Contract 1.1.0 adds `recent` (2026-05), `holdout` (2026-06) and `score` (2026-07) snapshots and a `monitoring`
block (`feature-spec.md` §9). Implement the monitoring module in your track:
1. **Reference:** the training rows of v1.0. Decile edges of each feature and of the deployed model's score.
2. **PSI** per post-deployment month: Σ (a − e) · ln(a / e), empty bins floored at 1e-4; < 0.10 stable, 0.10-0.25
   watch, ≥ 0.25 drift.
3. **Realised performance** of the deployed model on every labelled month: AUC, Brier, ECE, mean predicted vs observed.

The reference run on the 2026-07 export:

| Month | Role | AUC | ECE | Mean predicted | Observed churn | Drifted features |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-05 | recent | 0.771 | 0.049 | 9.1 % | 14.0 % | none (`tenure_months` on watch) |
| 2026-06 | holdout | 0.770 | 0.059 | 10.8 % | 16.7 % | `price_change_pct` (PSI 1.22, the June price rise) |
| 2026-07 | score | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | `tenure_months` (PSI 0.25) |

The ranking is as good as ever; the probabilities are far too low. Status: **retrain**.

<!-- track:python -->
Python: `churncast/monitoring.py` (`psi_edges`, `bin_shares`, `psi`, `monitor`, `calibration_offset`, `retrain`);
`np.searchsorted(edges, x, side="left")` = the number of edges strictly below x.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:sql -->
SQL: `sql/07_monitoring.sql` (decile edges with `quantile_cont`, shares, PSI, the holdout comparison); the runner

recalibration offset is `glm(y ~ 1, offset = eta, family = binomial)`.

steps.title: Champion versus challenger
steps.content_md:
The `retraining` block (§9): refit the champion's features on every labelled pre-deployment snapshot (train +
test, 17,010 rows), recalibrate the intercept on the `recent` month (offset +0.564), then compare on the `holdout`
month that neither model has seen:

| 2026-06 holdout | Champion v1.0.0 | Challenger |
|---|---|---|
| AUC | 0.770 | 0.773 (≥ 0.770 − 0.005 ✔) |
| Brier | 0.1188 | 0.1129 (better ✔) |
| ECE | 0.059 | 0.013 (≤ 0.03 ✔) |
| Age-band recall gap | 0.109 | 0.111 (≤ 0.15 ✔) |

Decision: **promote**. The challenger becomes `models/churncast-1.1.0.json` with `lineage.parent_model_version
1.0.0` and a `monitoring_reference` for next month. Check backwards compatibility: on the 2026-05 export the v1.1
pipeline must reproduce every v1.0 golden number (`parity.py --backcompat`), and the v1.0 API must load the 1.1 artefact.

steps.title: An observable API (v1.1)
steps.content_md:
Add to `serving/`: an `X-Request-ID` on every response (a caller's id is kept only if it is a safe token, else a
new one), one JSON log line per request (id, method, route template, status, duration; never the body, a customer
id or a key), `GET /metrics` in Prometheus text format (requests by route and status, a latency histogram,
predictions, explainer fallbacks by reason, the model version), and `model_version` + `request_id` in prediction
and explanation responses. v1.0 requests keep working unchanged. The smoke test grows to 10 checks.

2. Add a monitoring section to `docs/runbook.md`: what each alert means and who acts.
3. CHANGELOG 1.1.0, regenerate the model card, tag `v1.1.0`.

quiz.q: The July export fails `customers.channel.accepted`. What is the right fix?
options: Map `influencer` to `unknown` in the cleaning code
Turn the check into a warning
Investigate, then change the contract on purpose (add the value, bump to 1.1.0, keep 1.0.0 in history) and update all tracks and golden files
Delete the influencer customers
quiz.explanation: The check stopped the run because the world changed. The response is a reviewed decision recorded in the contract, not a silent workaround in code.

quiz.q: The deployed model's AUC is 0.770 on June but its ECE is 0.059. What does that mean?
options: The model is fine
It still ranks customers well, but its probabilities are too low (mean predicted 10.8 % vs 16.7 % observed): the call list works, the budget does not
The model must be replaced by the rule of thumb
The labels are wrong
quiz.explanation: Discrimination and calibration are different properties. A rise in the base rate shifts every probability; recalibrating the intercept fixes most of it.

quiz.q: What does a PSI of 1.22 for `price_change_pct` in June tell you?
options: The feature is broken
Customers churned because of the price change
The distribution of that feature moved strongly compared with training (a price rise), so the model sees inputs it rarely saw; investigate and check performance
The model is leaking
quiz.explanation: PSI measures distribution shift, not cause or harm. It is a signal to look at realised performance and the business context.

quiz.q: Why is the champion/challenger decision made on 2026-06 and not on 2026-05?
options: 2026-05 was used to recalibrate the challenger; deciding on the same month would favour it
2026-05 has no labels
2026-06 has more customers
The contract forbids 2026-05
quiz.explanation: Fit, calibrate and decide on different data. The holdout month is new to both models.

quiz.q: Which of these may the API's JSON access log contain?
options: The request body with the customer's features
The `LLM_API_KEY` used by the explainer
The request id, method, route template, status and duration
The customer id, to debug faster
quiz.explanation: Logs are kept long and read by many people. Log what you need to operate the service, never personal data or secrets.

quiz.q: What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
options: Nobody is told about the incident
It looks for the conditions and process gaps that allowed the incident, so people report problems openly, instead of naming a person to blame
It is written by someone outside the team
It has no action items
quiz.explanation: People make reasonable decisions with the information and tools they have. Fix the system (a contract change process, monitoring) so the next person cannot fall into the same gap.

recap: A versioned data contract turns an upstream change into a visible, reviewable decision.
Monitoring a live model: PSI drift for inputs and score, realised performance on labelled months, alerts with thresholds.
Discrimination versus calibration, and recalibration as a cheap fix for a shifted base rate.
Champion/challenger retraining with a pre-agreed gate on a holdout month, and backwards-compatible artefacts.
Operability: request ids, structured logs without personal data, metrics, and a blameless post-mortem.

phases.heading: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
phases.why_md:
Hiring managers do not read your code first; they read the first screen of your README and listen to how you talk
about trade-offs. A retrospective turns nine phases of work into lessons you can explain in an interview: what the
model is good for, what it cannot tell you, which decisions you would make again, and how AI helped and misled
you. In this phase you write the retrospective, put a case study at the top of your README, and prepare a
two-minute story and a portfolio blurb with real numbers.
objectives: Run a structured retrospective (what went well, what did not, what you would change) with evidence from your commits, CI runs and `AI_LOG.md`.
Write a README case study: problem, approach, results with numbers, limits, and how to run it in five minutes.
Explain the project's key trade-offs: logistic regression first, grouped out-of-time validation, calibration over accuracy, a contract that stops the run, three tracks.
Present the project in two minutes, including one thing that went wrong and what you changed.

challenger through the same gate, automated monthly monitoring).

quiz.q: A recruiter asks "how accurate is your model?". What is the best answer?
options: "About 91 % accurate"
"Accuracy is the wrong measure for a 9 % churn rate and a 10 % call list; it ranks well (test AUC 0.74), finds 30 % of next month's churners in the top 10 %, and its probabilities are calibrated"
"AUC 0.76 in cross-validation"
"It beats every other model"
quiz.explanation: Predicting "nobody churns" is 91 % accurate and useless. Use the metrics of the decision, from the out-of-time test.

quiz.q: What is the most important limitation to state about the ₹1.1 lakh monthly value?
options: It is in rupees
It depends on an assumed 25 % save rate; only a randomised hold-out experiment can measure whether calls cause customers to stay
It was computed in Python
It is a monthly figure
quiz.explanation: Predictive accuracy does not imply a causal effect of the intervention. State the assumption and how to test it.

quiz.q: Why mention the post-mortem in a portfolio?
options: To show the project failed
It shows you can operate a model after launch: detect a break, decide through a contract change, monitor, retrain and learn without blame
Post-mortems are required by GitHub
It makes the README longer
quiz.explanation: Most portfolio projects end at training. Handling drift and an upstream change is what production work looks like.

quiz.q: Which statement about the three tracks is the strongest interview point?
options: "I used three languages"
"Three independent implementations agreeing to 1e-6 caught a real tie-breaking bug that unit tests had missed"
"R is better than Python"
"SQL is faster"
quiz.explanation: Parity is a testing technique. Explain what it found, not just that it exists.

quiz.q: What belongs in "what I would do next"?
options: Nothing: the project is finished
Rewriting it in another language
A randomised hold-out to measure the save rate, uplift modelling, a more flexible challenger through the same gate, automated monthly monitoring
Removing the tests to make it simpler
quiz.explanation: Next steps should follow from the limitations you found, and keep the same evaluation discipline.

A README case study and a two-minute story that lead with the decision and the honest numbers.
How to talk about trade-offs: model choice, validation, calibration, fairness, causality, operations.

legacy_import.title: ChurnCast: End-to-End Data Science Case Study on Subscription Churn
legacy_import.description: TiffinBox, a meal-subscription startup, loses about 9 % of its paying customers every month, and its retention team can call only 10 % of them with an offer. Over nine phases you build the churn model they need, like a professional data science team: frame the decision and the label, write a data contract, a timeline and a modelling plan with ADRs, then build the pipeline test-first in your track: load four deliberately messy CSVs as text, apply documented cleaning rules that count every row they drop, check the contract, build point-in-time features that only use what was known at each month-end snapshot (and avoid the leaky cancellation_reason column), compare two baselines (the training churn rate and the team's five-flag rule) with two logistic regressions using grouped 5-fold cross-validation, then evaluate the champion once on out-of-time test months: AUC, average precision, Brier, calibration (ECE), precision and recall of the top-10 % call list, net value per month, slices, an age-band fairness check and a leakage scan, all behind a release gate. Golden files, invariants, leakage and contract-violation tests pin every number, and the Python, SQL and R tracks must agree (features to 1e-9, metrics and coefficients to 1e-6). CI executes the notebook or R Markdown report, runs the gate and checks parity; a generated model card and a FastAPI prediction API with an optional AI explainer (numbered facts in, guardrails out, a deterministic template as fallback) ship in Docker as v1.0.0. Then the model meets the real world: a new acquisition channel breaks the contract, prices change, and the deployed model's calibration slips. You version the contract, add drift (PSI) and realised-performance monitoring, recalibrate and retrain a challenger, decide champion vs challenger on a holdout month, add request ids, JSON logs and Prometheus metrics to the API, and write a blameless post-mortem (v1.1.0). Pick Python (pandas, scikit-learn, Jupyter), SQL (DuckDB) or R (tidymodels, R Markdown); the data, contract, golden files and API are shared. Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.
legacy_import.tech_stack: Python, SQL, R, pandas, scikit-learn, DuckDB, tidymodels, Jupyter, R Markdown, FastAPI, Docker, GitHub Actions

steps.title: Phase 0 · Setup and the brief
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A model nobody else can retrain is a rumour with a ROC curve. Professional data science teams start where
engineers start: a repository that installs with one command, data whose origin you can prove, tests that say what
"right" means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, read the brief and
the data, run the starter, meet the pending tests and the contract that will guide you, open your first pull
request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not train a single model yet, on purpose: first you learn which
decision the model serves and what the data can and cannot say.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
- Pick a track (Python, SQL or R), install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux, and run `make lint test`.
- Explain the brief in two sentences: who decides what each month, with which capacity, and what a wrong call costs.
- Prove the export in `data/raw/2026-05` is exactly the published one (`generate_data.py --check`) and list three defects you can see in the raw CSVs, plus the one column that must never become a feature.
- Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 0.1 · Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/ds-case-study` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**. The
   `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/ds-case-study.git
   cd ds-case-study
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/ds-case-study.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/ds-case-study`), not under `/mnt/c`.

### Step 0.2 · Install the tools for ONE track
Every track needs Git, `make` and Python 3.12+ (the data generator, the parity script, the gate and, later, the API
are Python). Run the doctor script; it tells you exactly what is missing:
```bash
scripts/doctor.sh
```

<!-- track:python -->
**Python track:** pandas, scikit-learn and Jupyter, installed into a virtual environment with exact versions.
```bash
cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv with the pinned versions
.venv/bin/python -c "import pandas, sklearn; print(pandas.__version__, sklearn.__version__)"
```
Open the notebook with `.venv/bin/jupyter lab notebooks/churn-model.ipynb` (or VS Code with the Jupyter
extension, selecting `.venv` as the kernel).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL track:** DuckDB, an in-process analytical database: no server, it reads the CSVs directly. Cleaning,
features, labels and every metric are written in `sql/*.sql`; a thin Python runner sets variables, does the one
thing SQL cannot (fitting the logistic regression, with scikit-learn) and writes the JSON files.
```bash
cd tracks/sql && make install        # .venv with duckdb, scikit-learn, sqlfluff, pytest
.venv/bin/python -c "import duckdb; print(duckdb.sql(\"SELECT count(*) FROM '../../data/raw/2026-05/invoices.csv'\"))"
```
Optional: the DuckDB CLI (`brew install duckdb`, or the binary from duckdb.org) to explore by hand.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:r -->
**R track:** R 4.6 with tidymodels (parsnip, rsample, yardstick), dplyr, testthat, lintr and R Markdown. The
toolchain is a **Docker image** pinned to a dated CRAN snapshot, so you, your reviewer and CI run exactly the same
