- [ ] `docker compose --profile train up` runs all three pipelines and parity MATCH.
- [ ] CHANGELOG 1.0.0, `docs/runbook.md`, the `v1.0.0` tag and its images on GHCR.
- [ ] An `AI_LOG.md` entry.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why is the model card generated from `metrics.json` and `model.json` instead of written by hand?
- [ ] Markdown is hard to write
- [x] Every number then comes from the model it describes, and CI's `--check` fails if the card and the model drift apart
- [ ] The site requires JSON
- [ ] It is shorter
> **Answer:** Hand-copied numbers go stale after the first retrain. The words around the numbers are reviewed in the script.

### Q2. The model card says the campaign is worth about ₹1.1 lakh a month. What is the biggest caveat?
- [ ] The prices are in rupees
- [x] It assumes a 25 % save rate that nobody has measured; a randomised hold-out group is needed to know whether calls cause customers to stay
- [ ] The AUC is too low
- [ ] It only covers the Python track
> **Answer:** A churn model predicts who is at risk, not who can be persuaded. The value estimate is only as good as the save-rate assumption.

### Q3. Which of these does the AI explainer receive?
- [ ] The customer id and their last three invoices
- [ ] The customer's age band, to personalise the message
- [x] Numbered facts: the probability, the base rate and the top feature contributions
- [ ] The whole training set
> **Answer:** Data minimisation by construction: the explainer can only talk about the facts it is given, and guardrails check that it did.

### Q4. The LLM answers "This customer will churn because of 3 late deliveries" but the fact says 2. What happens?
- [ ] The answer is returned as is
- [ ] The API returns 500
- [x] Two guardrails fail (a certainty claim and a number that is not in the facts), so the API returns the template with `fallback: true` and the reason
- [ ] The number is corrected automatically
> **Answer:** The API never shows an unchecked model answer. The template is always available, even when the provider is down.

### Q5. Why do the containers run as a non-root user with a read-only file system?
- [ ] It makes them faster
- [x] If the process is compromised, it cannot modify the image's code or write outside the mounted output and `/tmp`, which limits the damage
- [ ] Docker requires it
- [ ] So that the model cannot be retrained
> **Answer:** Least privilege applies to containers too. The compose file sets `read_only: true` and a `tmpfs` for `/tmp`; the images create uid 10001.

### Q6. Why can the API serve a `model.json` produced by the R track?
- [ ] The API contains an R interpreter
- [x] The artefact is a language-neutral JSON file defined by `contract/model.schema.json`: features, coefficients, means, threshold
- [ ] R models are converted to Python with a library
- [ ] It cannot; only Python models work
> **Answer:** A shared artefact contract decouples training from serving. The Docker job in CI proves it by serving the R model it just trained.

## 7. What you learned
- A model card that is generated, checked and honest about intended use, causality and limits.
- A small, validated prediction API with explanations that are exact for a linear model.
- A safe AI feature: data minimisation, guardrails, a deterministic fallback, offline by default, tested against a fake LLM.
- Docker images that are small, non-root and read-only, compose profiles, and continuous delivery to GHCR on a tag.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end      # = v1.0.0
git diff phase-5-end phase-6-end --stat
docker compose up -d --build && scripts/smoke-test.sh
```

steps.title: Phase 7 · Monitoring, drift, retraining and a post-mortem
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A model is evaluated once and then lives for months in a world that keeps changing. Marketing launches a new
channel, finance raises prices, churn rises, and a model that was well calibrated in March starts under-predicting
in June while its AUC still looks fine. In this phase the v1.0 model meets that world. The July export **breaks the
pipeline** (a new acquisition channel fails the data contract), and once that is fixed, monitoring shows drift and
a calibration problem. You version the contract, add drift (PSI) and realised-performance monitoring, retrain and
recalibrate a challenger, decide champion versus challenger on a month neither has seen, make the API observable
(request ids, JSON logs, metrics), and write a blameless post-mortem. That is v1.1.0.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Diagnose a contract failure from the exit code and the failing check, and fix it with a versioned contract change rather than a code hack.
- Compute the population stability index (PSI) of every feature and of the score against the training reference, and classify stable / watch / drift.
- Measure the deployed model's realised performance on newly labelled months, and explain why calibration can fail while AUC holds.
- Retrain and recalibrate a challenger, and promote it only through a pre-agreed champion/challenger gate on a holdout month.
- Add request ids, structured logs and Prometheus metrics to the API without logging personal data, and write a blameless post-mortem.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 7.1 · The July export breaks the pipeline
Take the new export from the reference and run v1.0 on it:
```bash
git checkout phase-7-end -- data/raw/2026-07
make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-07       # R: rdev make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-07
# contract error: contract check(s) failed: customers.channel.accepted      (exit 3)
```
Investigate before you fix: which value is new (`influencer`, launched by marketing in June 2026), how many
customers, since when. The contract did its job: it stopped a model from silently treating a new channel as
something else. Now decide **in the contract**, with a version bump to 1.1.0: add `influencer` to the accepted
values (the channel is not a model feature, so the model is unaffected; the slices and the fairness check see it).
Keep 1.0.0 in `contract/history/` and log the incident timeline for the post-mortem.

### Step 7.2 · Post-deployment snapshots and monitoring
Contract 1.1.0 adds `recent` (2026-05), `holdout` (2026-06) and `score` (2026-07) snapshots and a `monitoring`
block (`feature-spec.md` §9). Implement the monitoring module in your track:
1. **Reference:** the training rows of v1.0. Decile edges of each feature and of the deployed model's score.
2. **PSI** per post-deployment month: Σ (a − e) · ln(a / e), empty bins floored at 1e-4; < 0.10 stable, 0.10-0.25
   watch, ≥ 0.25 drift.
3. **Realised performance** of the deployed model on every labelled month: AUC, Brier, ECE, mean predicted vs observed.

The reference run on the 2026-07 export:

| Month | Role | AUC | ECE | Mean predicted | Observed churn | Drifted features |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-05 | recent | 0.771 | 0.049 | 9.1 % | 14.0 % | none (`tenure_months` on watch) |
| 2026-06 | holdout | 0.770 | 0.059 | 10.8 % | 16.7 % | `price_change_pct` (PSI 1.22, the June price rise) |
| 2026-07 | score | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | `tenure_months` (PSI 0.25) |

The ranking is as good as ever; the probabilities are far too low. Status: **retrain**.

<!-- track:python -->
Python: `churncast/monitoring.py` (`psi_edges`, `bin_shares`, `psi`, `monitor`, `calibration_offset`, `retrain`);
`np.searchsorted(edges, x, side="left")` = the number of edges strictly below x.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:sql -->
SQL: `sql/07_monitoring.sql` (decile edges with `quantile_cont`, shares, PSI, the holdout comparison); the runner
does the refit and the one-dimensional Newton steps of the recalibration, one aggregate query per step.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:r -->
R: `R/monitoring.R`; `findInterval(x, edges, left.open = TRUE)` counts the edges strictly below x, and the
recalibration offset is `glm(y ~ 1, offset = eta, family = binomial)`.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 7.3 · Champion versus challenger
The `retraining` block (§9): refit the champion's features on every labelled pre-deployment snapshot (train +
test, 17,010 rows), recalibrate the intercept on the `recent` month (offset +0.564), then compare on the `holdout`
month that neither model has seen:

| 2026-06 holdout | Champion v1.0.0 | Challenger |
|---|---|---|
| AUC | 0.770 | 0.773 (≥ 0.770 − 0.005 ✔) |
| Brier | 0.1188 | 0.1129 (better ✔) |
| ECE | 0.059 | 0.013 (≤ 0.03 ✔) |
| Age-band recall gap | 0.109 | 0.111 (≤ 0.15 ✔) |

Decision: **promote**. The challenger becomes `models/churncast-1.1.0.json` with `lineage.parent_model_version
1.0.0` and a `monitoring_reference` for next month. Check backwards compatibility: on the 2026-05 export the v1.1
pipeline must reproduce every v1.0 golden number (`parity.py --backcompat`), and the v1.0 API must load the 1.1 artefact.

### Step 7.4 · An observable API (v1.1)
Add to `serving/`: an `X-Request-ID` on every response (a caller's id is kept only if it is a safe token, else a
new one), one JSON log line per request (id, method, route template, status, duration; never the body, a customer
id or a key), `GET /metrics` in Prometheus text format (requests by route and status, a latency histogram,
predictions, explainer fallbacks by reason, the model version), and `model_version` + `request_id` in prediction
and explanation responses. v1.0 requests keep working unchanged. The smoke test grows to 10 checks.

### Step 7.5 · Post-mortem, runbook, release
1. Write `docs/postmortem-2026-07.md` (blameless): summary, impact (no wrong predictions shipped: the contract
   stopped the run), timeline, root cause (a new upstream value without a contract change process), what went well,
   what went badly (no monitoring until now: calibration had been off since May), action items with owners.
2. Add a monitoring section to `docs/runbook.md`: what each alert means and who acts.
3. CHANGELOG 1.1.0, regenerate the model card, tag `v1.1.0`.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Explain drift results to a stakeholder
```text
Here are the monitoring results of a churn model (no customer data): <paste the monitoring section of
metrics.json>. Explain to the Head of Growth in five sentences what changed, what it means for the call list and
for finance's budget, and what we propose. Distinguish clearly between "the ranking still works" and "the
probabilities are too low". No numbers that are not in the input.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every number against the JSON, and rejecting causal claims the data cannot
support (PSI says the price-change distribution moved; it does not say the price rise caused the extra churn).

### Prompt 2: Review my champion/challenger gate
```text
My retraining rule: refit on all labelled pre-deployment months, recalibrate the intercept on the most recent
labelled month, promote only if on a later holdout month AUC >= champion - 0.005, Brier < champion, ECE <= 0.03
and age-band recall gap <= 0.15. What could go wrong with this rule (leakage between calibration and holdout,
a holdout too small, repeated testing on the same month), and what would you change for a monthly cadence?
```
**Verify the output by:** checking that calibration and holdout months are different in your contract and code
(a test), and recording any change to the rule as a contract change with a version bump, not a code tweak.

### Prompt 3: Draft a blameless post-mortem
```text
Draft a blameless post-mortem from these facts: <paste your incident timeline, the failing check, the monitoring
table>. Sections: summary, impact, timeline (IST), root cause (5 whys), what went well, what went badly, action
items (owner, due date). No blame on individuals; focus on process and systems.
```
**Verify the output by:** matching every timestamp and number to your log and `metrics.json`, removing invented
details (an assistant may add an outage or a customer complaint that did not happen), and making each action item
testable.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] Contract 1.1.0 (with 1.0.0 in `contract/history/`), the 2026-07 export, golden files for 2026-07.
- [ ] Monitoring and retraining in your track; tests green; parity MATCH on 2026-07 and backcompat MATCH on 2026-05.
- [ ] `models/churncast-1.1.0.json` promoted by the gate, model card regenerated.
- [ ] API 1.1 with request ids, JSON logs and `/metrics`; 10/10 smoke checks.
- [ ] `docs/postmortem-2026-07.md`, runbook monitoring section, CHANGELOG 1.1.0, tag `v1.1.0`.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. The July export fails `customers.channel.accepted`. What is the right fix?
- [ ] Map `influencer` to `unknown` in the cleaning code
- [ ] Turn the check into a warning
- [x] Investigate, then change the contract on purpose (add the value, bump to 1.1.0, keep 1.0.0 in history) and update all tracks and golden files
- [ ] Delete the influencer customers
> **Answer:** The check stopped the run because the world changed. The response is a reviewed decision recorded in the contract, not a silent workaround in code.

### Q2. The deployed model's AUC is 0.770 on June but its ECE is 0.059. What does that mean?
- [ ] The model is fine
- [x] It still ranks customers well, but its probabilities are too low (mean predicted 10.8 % vs 16.7 % observed): the call list works, the budget does not
- [ ] The model must be replaced by the rule of thumb
- [ ] The labels are wrong
> **Answer:** Discrimination and calibration are different properties. A rise in the base rate shifts every probability; recalibrating the intercept fixes most of it.

### Q3. What does a PSI of 1.22 for `price_change_pct` in June tell you?
- [ ] The feature is broken
- [ ] Customers churned because of the price change
- [x] The distribution of that feature moved strongly compared with training (a price rise), so the model sees inputs it rarely saw; investigate and check performance
- [ ] The model is leaking
> **Answer:** PSI measures distribution shift, not cause or harm. It is a signal to look at realised performance and the business context.

### Q4. Why is the champion/challenger decision made on 2026-06 and not on 2026-05?
- [x] 2026-05 was used to recalibrate the challenger; deciding on the same month would favour it
- [ ] 2026-05 has no labels
- [ ] 2026-06 has more customers
- [ ] The contract forbids 2026-05
> **Answer:** Fit, calibrate and decide on different data. The holdout month is new to both models.

### Q5. Which of these may the API's JSON access log contain?
- [ ] The request body with the customer's features
- [ ] The `LLM_API_KEY` used by the explainer
- [x] The request id, method, route template, status and duration
- [ ] The customer id, to debug faster
> **Answer:** Logs are kept long and read by many people. Log what you need to operate the service, never personal data or secrets.

### Q6. What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
- [ ] Nobody is told about the incident
- [x] It looks for the conditions and process gaps that allowed the incident, so people report problems openly, instead of naming a person to blame
- [ ] It is written by someone outside the team
- [ ] It has no action items
> **Answer:** People make reasonable decisions with the information and tools they have. Fix the system (a contract change process, monitoring) so the next person cannot fall into the same gap.

## 7. What you learned
- A versioned data contract turns an upstream change into a visible, reviewable decision.
- Monitoring a live model: PSI drift for inputs and score, realised performance on labelled months, alerts with thresholds.
- Discrimination versus calibration, and recalibration as a cheap fix for a shifted base rate.
- Champion/challenger retraining with a pre-agreed gate on a holdout month, and backwards-compatible artefacts.
- Operability: request ids, structured logs without personal data, metrics, and a blameless post-mortem.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-8 phase-7-end      # = v1.1.0
git diff phase-6-end phase-7-end --stat
(cd tracks/python && make run DATA=../../data/raw/2026-05 OUT=out/2026-05)
python3 scripts/parity.py --backcompat contract/golden/metrics-2026-05.json tracks/python/out/2026-05/metrics.json
```

steps.title: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Hiring managers do not read your code first; they read the first screen of your README and listen to how you talk
about trade-offs. A retrospective turns nine phases of work into lessons you can explain in an interview: what the
model is good for, what it cannot tell you, which decisions you would make again, and how AI helped and misled
you. In this phase you write the retrospective, put a case study at the top of your README, and prepare a
two-minute story and a portfolio blurb with real numbers.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Run a structured retrospective (what went well, what did not, what you would change) with evidence from your commits, CI runs and `AI_LOG.md`.
- Write a README case study: problem, approach, results with numbers, limits, and how to run it in five minutes.
- Explain the project's key trade-offs: logistic regression first, grouped out-of-time validation, calibration over accuracy, a contract that stops the run, three tracks.
- Present the project in two minutes, including one thing that went wrong and what you changed.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 8.1 · Collect the evidence
```bash
git log --oneline phase-0-end..phase-7-end | wc -l          # how many commits
git log --format='%s' phase-2-end..phase-3-end | head -20    # what M1-M5 really took
gh run list --branch solution --limit 10                     # CI history (or the Actions tab)
```
Re-read your `AI_LOG.md`: count the entries where you kept, changed and rejected an AI output. Find the one
rejection that saved you the most (a leak, a wrong metric, an invented number).

### Step 8.2 · The retrospective
Write `docs/retrospective.md` with: the goal and what was delivered (v1.0.0, v1.1.0); results (test AUC, ECE, the
call list against the rule, the value estimate and its assumption, fairness); what went well; what went badly and
what you changed; decisions you would make again and ones you would not; how AI helped and where it misled you;
what you would do next (a randomised hold-out to measure the real save rate, uplift modelling, a gradient-boosted
challenger through the same gate, automated monthly monitoring).

### Step 8.3 · The README case study
Put a short case study right below the badges of `README.md`: the problem in two sentences, the approach in four
bullets, a results table (baseline vs model), the most important limitation, and "run it in five minutes". The
reference version is at `phase-8-end`. Numbers must come from your `metrics.json`; link the model card and the
post-mortem.

### Step 8.4 · Your two-minute story and the blurb
Practise out loud: the decision (10 % call capacity), the trap (leakage, a random split), the model and why
(calibrated, explainable), the result versus the rule (AUC 0.743 vs 0.651, recall of the call list 30 % vs 21 %),
what happened after launch (contract break, calibration drift, a recalibrated challenger promoted on a holdout),
and one thing you would do differently. Then adapt the portfolio blurb in `cms/project.json` for your CV or
LinkedIn; keep every number one you can defend.

<!-- track:python -->
Python track: link the executed notebook (download the `report-python` artifact of the last green run, or use
nbviewer on your fork) from the case study.
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:sql -->
SQL track: link `out/report.md` (from the `report-sql` artifact) and one SQL file you are proud of (the
point-in-time features of `03_features.sql` are a good interview topic).
<!-- /track -->
<!-- track:r -->
R track: link the knitted `churn-model.html` (from the `report-r` artifact, or GitHub Pages on your fork) and mention
the pinned Docker toolchain; reproducibility is a strong interview topic.
<!-- /track -->

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Run my retrospective interview
```text
Interview me about a churn-modelling project I just finished, one question at a time, as a senior data scientist
would in a retrospective. Ask about decisions, trade-offs, mistakes and what I would do differently. After 8
questions, summarise my answers as a retrospective with sections: went well, went badly, would change, next steps.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking that the summary only contains what you said (assistants fill gaps with generic
lessons), and backing each point with a commit, a CI run or an `AI_LOG.md` entry.

### Prompt 2: Tighten my README case study
```text
Here is the case study at the top of my README: <paste>. Make it readable in 60 seconds by a hiring manager:
problem, approach, results, limits, how to run. Keep every number exactly as it is, do not add new claims, and
point out any claim that is not supported by a number or a link.
```
**Verify the output by:** diffing the numbers before and after (none may change), and checking every link.

### Prompt 3: Mock interview on trade-offs
```text
Ask me five hard interview questions about this project: <paste the case study>. Focus on leakage, validation,
calibration, fairness, the value estimate's assumptions, and why logistic regression. After each answer, tell me
what a strong answer would add.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each "strong answer" against `feature-spec.md`, the model card and your
results; reject advice that contradicts your own evidence (e.g. "always use XGBoost").

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `docs/retrospective.md` with evidence.
- [ ] A README case study at the top of `README.md`, every number from `metrics.json`.
- [ ] Your two-minute story (written or recorded) and an adapted portfolio blurb.
- [ ] A final `AI_LOG.md` entry: how AI helped and misled you over the whole project.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. A recruiter asks "how accurate is your model?". What is the best answer?
- [ ] "About 91 % accurate"
- [x] "Accuracy is the wrong measure for a 9 % churn rate and a 10 % call list; it ranks well (test AUC 0.74), finds 30 % of next month's churners in the top 10 %, and its probabilities are calibrated"
- [ ] "AUC 0.76 in cross-validation"
- [ ] "It beats every other model"
> **Answer:** Predicting "nobody churns" is 91 % accurate and useless. Use the metrics of the decision, from the out-of-time test.

### Q2. What is the most important limitation to state about the ₹1.1 lakh monthly value?
- [ ] It is in rupees
- [x] It depends on an assumed 25 % save rate; only a randomised hold-out experiment can measure whether calls cause customers to stay
- [ ] It was computed in Python
- [ ] It is a monthly figure
> **Answer:** Predictive accuracy does not imply a causal effect of the intervention. State the assumption and how to test it.

### Q3. Why mention the post-mortem in a portfolio?
- [ ] To show the project failed
- [x] It shows you can operate a model after launch: detect a break, decide through a contract change, monitor, retrain and learn without blame
- [ ] Post-mortems are required by GitHub
- [ ] It makes the README longer
> **Answer:** Most portfolio projects end at training. Handling drift and an upstream change is what production work looks like.

### Q4. Which statement about the three tracks is the strongest interview point?
- [ ] "I used three languages"
- [x] "Three independent implementations agreeing to 1e-6 caught a real tie-breaking bug that unit tests had missed"
- [ ] "R is better than Python"
- [ ] "SQL is faster"
> **Answer:** Parity is a testing technique. Explain what it found, not just that it exists.

### Q5. What belongs in "what I would do next"?
- [ ] Nothing: the project is finished
- [ ] Rewriting it in another language
- [x] A randomised hold-out to measure the save rate, uplift modelling, a more flexible challenger through the same gate, automated monthly monitoring
- [ ] Removing the tests to make it simpler
> **Answer:** Next steps should follow from the limitations you found, and keep the same evaluation discipline.

## 7. What you learned
- A retrospective grounded in evidence from commits, CI runs and the AI log.
- A README case study and a two-minute story that lead with the decision and the honest numbers.
- How to talk about trade-offs: model choice, validation, calibration, fairness, causality, operations.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git diff phase-7-end phase-8-end -- README.md docs/retrospective.md
git switch -c my-portfolio phase-8-end
```
